sections.overview: The yellow-footed tortoise is a large land tortoise native to tropical South America. Its scientific name is Chelonoidis denticulatus; older names include C. denticulata and Geochelone denticulata. It lives chiefly in humid forest and searches the ground for fallen foods and shelter. Field knowledge comes mainly from a few studied sites.
sections.identification: Adult yellow-footed tortoises usually have a carapace length of about 35 cm (reported range 29–44 cm) and mass around 6 kg (2.5–14 kg); exceptional records reach roughly 70 cm and 50 kg. Males have a concave plastron, while the female plastron is flatter or convex. These ranges are broad and the extreme values are uncommon. Its rounded, domed carapace is bone covered by horny scutes, above a flatter plastron. The shell is brown, often with pale yellow or orange scute centers; yellow-orange scales mark the head and limbs. This pattern helps separate it from the red-footed tortoise (Chelonoidis carbonarius), but colors vary and should not be used alone. Adult males have a longer, thicker tail and a somewhat concave plastron. The species is generally larger, though size also varies by region. Elongated prefrontal scales on the head are another useful distinction from the smaller, fragmented scales typical of red-footed tortoises.
sections.habitat: The species is associated mainly with humid tropical forests, including Amazonian rainforest. It shelters in leaf litter, beneath fallen logs and among roots or dense plants, which buffer heat and drying. In a six-month Central Amazon study, tortoises usually sheltered when encountered; smaller animals often used leaf litter. Tracked individuals used an average 1.56 hectares, with larger areas used by larger tortoises. This local estimate is not a universal home range.
sections.diet: This opportunistic omnivore gathers food mainly from the forest floor: fallen fruits, flowers, seeds, fungi, invertebrates and carrion. A Brazilian study found seeds of several plants in tortoise droppings, many still viable; a later study of two Chelonoidis species found viable seeds in most samples. Seeds can therefore survive gut passage, but germination and successful plant recruitment are not guaranteed.
sections.behavior: Field accounts describe mostly daytime activity, though weather and local conditions affect when tortoises move. As reptiles they depend on external heat; shade, humid refuges and sunlit patches offer different thermal conditions, but detailed seasonal thermoregulation is poorly studied in this species. In Central Amazonia, animals were encountered sheltering much more often than walking or feeding. Studies document individual movements and shelter use, not a stable social-group system.
sections.reproduction: Wild breeding is opportunistic and seasonal. In 347 adult females from the Peruvian Amazon, reproductive stages occurred through the year, but output varied with climate: follicle growth tracked peak rainfall and laying was estimated mainly in the dry season. Gravid females held an average 3.7 shelled eggs; estimated clutch size averaged 5.1, with a wide range. These figures come from one harvested population. Wild incubation duration and hatchling survival remain poorly documented.
sections.ecology: By eating fruit and moving through forest, the tortoise can carry seeds away from parent plants. A 2025 study of two Chelonoidis species combined fecal samples, seed tests and movement data; its models placed many seeds hundreds of metres away, sometimes beyond a kilometre. This supports a dispersal role, but the effect on plants depends on where seeds land and whether they germinate and establish.
sections.conservation: The 1996 global IUCN assessment classified the tortoise as Vulnerable, a historical result rather than a recent measurement. In December 2025, the IUCN specialist group listed an Endangered assessment among those submitted and in press, without giving its assessment date. The tortoise is hunted for meat and enters international live-animal trade. A Norwegian scientific review reports depletion and scarcity in some populations, while noting uncertainty about captive breeding in trade. Conditions vary across its range and need local monitoring.
